sweep_summary: All five works with stress in the title for Hiw are keyword noise from 'ambiguity' (English/Korean/Dutch sentence-prosody and metrical papers: Beach 1991, Lee & Watson 2011, Snedeker & Trueswell 2003, Jones 2016, Lowenstamm & van der Wilt 1982); none concerns Hiw and none was downloaded. The catalog's deciding source, François 2010 Phonology 27(3) sec. 2.2 (pp..) and its stress statement was re-read verbatim: primary stress on the last non-schwa vowel, schwa-only words unpredictable, secondary stress on alternate vowels leftward; the catalog quote and locator are exact. Supplementary reading this search of works with stress in the title: François 2005 OL 44(2) p. 451 (held under leha1244) states that in essentially all Torres-Banks languages words are now stressed on their final rather than penultimate syllable, which confirms without refining; the Pangloss Hiw presentation page (downloaded, saved) and the Wikipedia page (downloaded. paraphrases François 2010) add nothing first-hand. The author's publication list (downloaded) shows no Hiw grammar, dictionary or other prosody paper; the only unread item is the unpublished François 2009 ms. 'Stress-driven sonority in Hiw' (low priority, author-only). no reclassification needed.

new_statements.locator: sec. 2.2 'Stress', pp. 397-398 (the text layer), exx. (5)-(7) and fn. 3
new_statements.reading: Primary stress on the rightmost non-schwa vowel (so final if the last vowel is full, otherwise penultimate/antepenultimate as far as the final schwa string extends); words whose only vowels are schwa have lexically unpredictable stress; secondary stress on alternate vowels leftward. This is a vowel-quality (schwa vs. full) conditioned right-edge system, consistent with the catalog's 'weight' coding in the broad sense (schwa-sensitive, final-schwa extrametricality). No newer first-hand statement exists; the same author's 2005 OL paper (p. 451) states the area-wide shift to final stress and is consistent.

audit.quote_check: confirmed in the copy we hold
audit.reasoning: Quote verified verbatim at the stated locator in the publisher PDF we hold. The deciding source is a 2010 peer-reviewed Phonology article by the language's sole describer, and it is the most extensive phonological description that exists (Glottolog Glottolog's most extensive description confirms no grammar/sketch; author's publication list confirms no later Hiw phonology or prosody work). The classification — quality-sensitive 'last full (non-schwa) vowel' primary stress, unbounded (ex. 5d [ˈwOtəjə] skips two schwa syllables), lexical stress only in all-schwa words, alternating secondary stress leftward counting schwa — matches the source exactly. Only conceivable upgrade is the author's unpublished 2009 stress ms, which is not accessible; no action needed.

sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: Stress is predictable in Hiw, except in the case of words which only contain /ə/. Generally, primary stress falls on the last syllable which does not contain /ə/. For example: [mɔˈwɪ] 'moon', [ˈwɔtəjə] 'maybe'. In the case of words whose only vowel is schwa, stress is unpredictable: thus [βəˈjə] 'pandanus leaf' is oxytone and [ˈtəpjə] 'dish' is paroxytone.
sources.note: Secondary paraphrase of François 2010: 'Stress is predictable in Hiw, except in the case of words which only contain /ə/. Generally, primary stress falls on the last syllable which does not contain /ə/.. Polysyllabic words have secondary stress, which falls on every second syllable from the primary stressed syllable, going leftwards.' Adds nothing beyond the deciding source.

sources.citation: François, Alexandre (2005). Unraveling the history of the vowels of seventeen northern Vanuatu languages. Oceanic Linguistics 44(2): 443-504.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: The loss of word-final posttonic vowels explains why, in essentially all the languages of the area, words are now systematically stressed on their final rather than their penultimate syllable (contra Lynch 2000:77). Exactly the same evolution is attested in modern French: due to the progressive loss of all etymological posttonic vowels, French has become a perfectly oxytone language.
sources.note: Area-wide statement covering Hiw (one of the 17 languages, listed as 'Hiu'): loss of post-tonic final vowels made words final-stressed. p. 451: 'The loss of word-final posttonic vowels explains why, in essentially all the languages of the area, words are now systematically stressed on their final rather than their penultimate syllable (contra Lynch 2000:77).' Consistent with the catalog's 2010 rule (stress on last non-schwa vowel), but it is a historical-comparative generalisation, not a Hiw-specific description; the 2010 article remains the deciding source.
